questions.q: By default, what data can an Apex test method see?
options: Every record currently in the org
Only records the test method itself creates (plus certain unavoidable setup data)
Only records created in the last 24 hours
Only records owned by the running user's manager
questions.explain: Apex tests are data-isolated by default: a test method sees none of the org's pre-existing data unless it creates that data itself, or the test is explicitly marked @isTest(SeeAllData=true).

options: It doubles the governor limits available to the test
It gives the test visibility into the org's existing data, bypassing normal test data isolation
It forces the test to run twice for reliability
It automatically generates a test factory for every object
questions.explain: SeeAllData=true opts a test into seeing real org data. It's discouraged for everyday use because it makes tests less portable and, as covered in Lesson 6, it's incompatible with @TestSetup methods.

questions.q: What problem does a test factory (test data builder) method primarily solve?
options: It eliminates the need for any assertions in a test
It removes the need for the 75% code coverage requirement
It avoids duplicating the same record-construction code across many test methods
It automatically deletes test data from production
questions.explain: Without a factory, the same field-by-field record construction gets copy-pasted into every test method; a factory centralizes that construction so a new required field only needs fixing in one place.

questions.q: A TestDataFactory.createContacts(accountId, count) method takes a count parameter and returns a list. Why is this design more useful than a method that always returns exactly one hardcoded Contact?
options: It has no real advantage over a hardcoded single record
The same factory method can serve both a single-record test and a bulk test with many records, without changing the factory
Returning a list is required by the Apex compiler for all factory methods
It automatically satisfies the governor limit on DML rows
questions.explain: A flexible factory that accepts a count can build exactly as many records as a given test scenario needs — one for a simple test, or hundreds for a bulk test like the trigger tests in Lesson 8.

questions.q: Which approach does this lesson recommend over building one factory method with a dozen optional parameters trying to cover every scenario?
options: Always use SeeAllData=true instead of factories
A few small, clearly named factory methods for distinct scenarios
Never use factory methods, only inline construction
Store all test data in custom metadata instead of Apex
questions.explain: The lesson recommends several small, well-named factory methods (createAccount, createHighValueOpportunity, etc.) over one sprawling method trying to handle every possible case.
